title: What does the placenta do?
description: Understanding the vital functions of the placenta in supporting your pēpi's growth and development throughout pregnancy.

contentSections.title: Placenta
contentSections.content:
The placenta (whenua) is grown by your pēpi from the very start of pregnancy. It plays essential roles in helping your body adapt to support pregnancy . The placenta makes hormones and sends signals that can change how your heart, blood vessels, and immune system work.

The placenta's other very important job is to take up nutrients and oxygen from your blood and transport them to your pēpi, while also removing waste products from pēpi's blood back into your body (where your body will process them and remove them through your breath or when you go to the bathroom).

Your placenta comes out after your pēpi and is around 20 cm wide - the size of a frisbee. Not all placentae are round, and even unusual-looking placentae can do a great job at growing a healthy pēpi.

Whilst it might appear like a solid organ if you see it after delivery, the placenta is actually built like a complex and bushy tree, as shown below.

Mother's blood flows around the outside of the tree, whilst pēpi's blood flows in blood vessels inside the branches. This means your bloodstream never mixes with your pēpi's; instead, nutrients and oxygen pass across the outer layer of the placenta.

The branching tree structure means that the placenta has a huge surface– if the surface were stretched out, it would be as large as half a tennis court.

Some of the most important parts of placental development happen early in pregnancy (in the first trimester), when the foundations of the placenta's structure are laid down. This makes early pregnancy a very important time to establish a healthy pregnancy.
